pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1). ROTE COUNTING to 100 — reciting the number-word sequence fluently, forwards and backwards, from 0, 1, or any given number, by ones. Gelman & Gallistel's STABLE-ORDER principle in action; the verbal spine that object counting, place value and skip counting all run on.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 verbatim — 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'. Non-statutory guidance distinguishes 'counting as reciting numbers' from 'counting as enumerating objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'Count to 100 by ones and by tens'; K.CC.2 'Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).'
• Operational details: Build a stable ordered list at least as long as needed (Thompson: you can't count seven items if your names stop at six). Target the two hard spots — the irregular TEENS (eleven, twelve, thirteen, not 'oneteen') and the DECADE BOUNDARIES (…28, 29 → 30; 39 → 40) where children stall or invent 'twenty-ten'. Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are harder and must be practised explicitly. Use the HUNDRED SQUARE to expose the repeating 0–9 ones pattern down each column so counting becomes pattern, not just memory.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) rote counts forward 0→~30 without skipping/repeating and recites the teens correctly. Tier B (5–6) counts to 100 forward and back from 20→0, bridging decade boundaries. Tier C (6) starts a forward OR backward count from any given number (e.g. 'from 67') and predicts the number after a decade boundary.
bestPractices: Practise oral counting daily and rhythmically (chants, songs, choral counting); little and often builds the stable list.
Target decade boundaries and irregular teens explicitly — rehearse '…29, 30…' and '…39, 40…' as named hurdles where the sequence breaks down.
Practise BACKWARD counting and starting from any number separately (much harder than forward-from-one) — essential for later counting-back subtraction.
Use a hundred square / number track so the ones-digit cycle (0–9 repeating) and the new-row-per-decade structure are SEEN, converting recall into prediction.
Distinguish reciting the sequence from counting objects — keep both, but name which you are doing.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (rows of ten; a column shares a ones digit).
Counting songs, rhymes and choral chant (the aural sequence).
A pointer/marker moving along the track as the class counts.
commonMisconceptions: Decade-boundary stalls: '…28, 29, twenty-ten' or jumping to the wrong decade — the ones-cycle-to-next-ten transition isn't secured.
Irregular teens: 'eleventeen', or mapping teen words to the wrong quantity; hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
Counting forward from one but not backward or from a mid-point — the sequence is stored as a single forward chant.
Confusing rote reciting with meaningful counting — chanting numbers with nothing attached and assuming that IS counting.

learn.summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) rote counting to (and across) 100: reciting the number-word sequence fluently by ones — forwards and backwards, beginning from 0, 1, or any given number. The aim is to build a stable, repeatable ordered list of number words that object counting, place value and skip counting later run on, while distinguishing reciting the sequence from counting objects. Target the two predictable break points: the irregular teens (eleven, twelve, thirteen — not 'oneteen') and the decade boundaries (…28, 29 → 30; …39 → 40). Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are harder than forward-from-one and must be practised explicitly. A hundred square exposes the repeating 0–9 ones pattern so counting becomes prediction, not pure memory.

activities.title: Predict across the decade boundary on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner says 'twenty-ten' or 'sixty-ten' at a boundary, do NOT re-drill the whole 1–100 sequence. Target just the seam where the error happened (e.g. 68, 69, 70 for 'sixty-ten'; 28, 29, 30 for 'twenty-ten'), plus similar seams such as 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.

If a learner jumps to the wrong decade (…39, 50), show that after 39 the count moves to the next ten, 40, not 50. Point to where 40 sits on the chart being used: on a 1–100 square it is the last cell of the 31–40 row, and 50 ends the row below; on a 0–99 square 40 starts its row. Ask which number comes straight after 39, so the learner sees that the tens go up by just one ten.
When a prediction is correct, name the pattern aloud: 'the ones went 7, 8, 9 and then started again at 0, and the tens went up by one ten.'
activities.rationale: Decade boundaries and irregular teen words are the predictable places the oral sequence breaks down; a hundred square makes the repeating ones-cycle and ten-per-row decade structure visible, which can turn recall into prediction. A visible marker, forward/back movement, start-anywhere entry and optional say-back audio make the counting mechanism concrete; these are illustrative interactions, not required ones — a static hundred square or a paper number track pointed at cell by cell can serve the same teaching purpose with less automation.
sourceClaims: Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
Decade boundaries and irregular teen words are the predictable break points in the oral sequence; the hundred square exposes the repeating structure.
learnerActions: Point to a chosen starting cell on a hundred square (e.g. 67) and count on aloud, moving a pointer or marker cell by cell: '68, 69…'
As you approach a decade boundary, pause and predict the next number BEFORE saying it ('after 69 comes…?') and check whether the tens goes up by one ten (to 70) rather than inventing 'sixty-ten'.
Trace down a single column and say the numbers aloud to notice the ones digit stays the same while the tens digit climbs.
Repeat for the rehearsed seams: 28, 29, 30 and 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.
Then run the marker the other way to count backward across a boundary (e.g. 41, 40, 39…).
activities.intendedInsight: 100 numbers are not 100 separate things to memorise: the ones digits cycle through 0–9 again and again (on a 1–100 square each row runs from 1 to 10, e.g. 31–40; on a 0–99 square from 0 to 9, e.g. 40–49). So once you know the repeating ones pattern, the decade words and the irregular teens, and can cross cleanly into the next ten, most of the sequence becomes predictable.

activities.title: Start anywhere and keep going
feedback: If a learner restarts at 1 when asked to begin at 23, do NOT treat it as an error to penalise — it matures with practice; play 'start here and keep going' from many points using a visible track.

If backward counting is halting, skips, or reverts to forward, do NOT expect it to arrive alongside forward counting. Practise short backward runs separately with a number line before building up to 20→0, then to longer backward runs from any given number up to 100.
Keep runs short and slow when the word string itself is insecure; point to each number rather than drilling at speed.
activities.rationale: Starting mid-sequence and counting backward develop separately from, and later than, forward-from-one counting, so they warrant explicit dedicated practice; backward counting also underpins later counting-back subtraction. A number line or track gives a visible referent for entry points and direction.
sourceClaims: Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
K.CC.1 'Count to 100 by ones and by tens'; K.CC.2 'Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).'
learnerActions: On being given a starting number (e.g. 'start at 23'), begin the count there and continue forward WITHOUT going back to 1 first.
Practise entering the sequence from many different points — a visible number track or hundred square can mark where to begin.
Count on and across 100 to see the sequence continues (what comes after 100?), consistent with the 'to and across 100' standard.

Count backward from a given number: begin with short runs (e.g. 5 down to 0, then 15 down to 0) as scaffolds, then build up to 20 down to 0 without gaps, and on towards the full target of counting back from any given number up to 100 (e.g. 100 down to 90, 73 down to 60), including across decade boundaries. Use a number line or hundred square and, if helpful, a physical step-down for each number.
activities.intendedInsight: The number-word list should be accessible from any point and in both directions, not only as a single forward chant started at one.

activities.title: Daily rhythmic oral counting and take-turns buddy counting
feedback: If a learner says 'eleventeen' or maps a teen word to the wrong quantity, slow down and rehearse the teen stretch explicitly, distinguishing 'thirteen' from 'thirty' by sound.
Reinforce that chanting numbers with nothing attached is reciting the sequence, not counting objects — name which one you are doing each time.
Praise accurate turn-taking production, not just recognition of the right number when it is shown.
activities.rationale: Little-and-often oral practice builds the stable ordered list. The stable-order principle requires the words to be produced in the same order every time, and accurate object counting also needs the list to be at least as long as the set being counted. Take-turns oral dialogue is a legitimate oral-fluency drill here because the objective is verbal production; it does not make the ones-cycle pattern visible, so it complements rather than replaces hundred-square work.
sourceClaims: Stable-order principle: counting words must be said in a repeatable order, and the list must be at least as long as the set to be counted.
Year 1 verbatim: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; guidance distinguishes counting as reciting from counting as enumerating objects.
learnerActions: Count aloud daily in short, rhythmic bursts — chants, songs or choral counting with the class or an adult.
Take turns with a partner (or a count-with-me buddy): you say one number, they say the next, alternating up the sequence.
When the buddy deliberately stumbles at a decade boundary ('…29… twenty-ten?'), catch and correct it.
Rehearse the irregular teens as a named stretch (eleven, twelve, thirteen…) and check you are not hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
activities.intendedInsight: The oral number sequence is built little and often, as sound and rhythm; taking turns and fixing a buddy's stumble makes the learner produce and monitor the sequence rather than just hear it.

activities.title: Fill the gap and fix the sequence (retrieval practice)
feedback: If an isolated number is missing or doubled, do NOT drill at speed — slow the pace and anchor on a hundred square, pointing to each; if the word string is broken, rebuild it gently rather than penalising.
Use gap-fill and ordering items as retrieval checks after oral and pattern work, not as the first teaching step.
activities.rationale: Short constructed-response items (fill the missing number, order steps, count back) give retrieval practice and surface specific breaks — but they check production of remembered numbers rather than teach the pattern, so they sit after the pattern and oral activities.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing number in a sequence (e.g. _, 29, _) and say what comes after 29 (30) and what comes just before 60 (59).
Put jumbled number cards back into order.
Count back a set number of steps from a given start.
Spot and fix a recite that has an omitted or doubled number (…14, 15, 17…).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure rote counting means you can enter, continue, reverse and repair the sequence — not only chant it from the start.

constraints: Reciting the number sequence is not the same as counting objects; keep both and name which is being done so chanting with nothing attached is not mistaken for enumeration.

Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are genuinely harder than forward-from-one and develop later; restarting at 1 or halting backward counting are developmental stages to practise, not errors to penalise.
Recognition or multiple-choice items check remembered numbers but do not elicit independent oral production of the sequence; include spoken recite tasks so the learner constructs the sequence aloud.
A hundred square makes the ones-cycle and decade structure visible, which supports prediction, but it does not by itself build oral fluency — pair it with daily spoken counting.
A static hundred square works as a reference chart (tap/point → number) but cannot itself drive a start-anywhere or backward count; the adult or learner must direct that movement.
Build the ordered list at least as long as needed before expecting accurate object counting over that range (you cannot count seven items if the names stop at six).
Distinguish 'thirteen' from 'thirty' and similar teen/decade pairs explicitly, as they are easily confused by sound.
The cited NC standard is 'to and across 100'; a little counting past 100 is within that standard, not off-objective, even though the short title says 'to 100'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's claim that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that conversation is 'the one topic where dialogue-as-drill has real value' are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts; retained here only as the narrowly scoped observation that oral turn-taking suits an oral-production objective while a hundred square better shows pattern.
The NCETM hundred-square/early-number source is marked verified:false in the row; the pattern-visibility rationale drawing on it should be treated as unconfirmed.

The row is internally inconsistent on range: the parentTitle/description say 'to 100' while the quoted NC standard says 'count to and across 100'. Counting a little across 100 is therefore within the cited standard — a natural continuation showing the sequence does not stop at 100 — not an off-objective extension.

Whether the 69→70 (or 67→70) transition is literally a 'new row' depends on the hundred-square layout used (0–99 vs 1–100); the ones-cycle-and-increment-the-tens point holds regardless, so the inherited 'new row' wording is kept but should be matched to the actual square shown to the child.

probeDeeper: Start at 47 and count on for me.
Keep going past 100 — what comes after 100?
assess.correctAnswer: Recites 1–100 in order with no omissions or repeats, crosses each decade boundary cleanly (…29, 30…; …49, 50…), resumes forward from 23 without restarting at 1, and counts back 20→0 without gaps.

errorPatterns.pattern: decade-boundary breakdown — stalls or errs at the ten-crossing ('…29, twenty-ten', or jumps '…39, 50') because the -ty transition isn't fluent
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT re-drill the whole 1–100 sequence — target just the seams: rehearse 28,29,30 / 38,39,40 with a hundred square until the bridges are automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: hesitation or error specifically at 29→30, 39→40, etc., while within-decade counting is fine

errorPatterns.pattern: can't enter mid-sequence — asked to start at 23, goes back to 1 and counts up to reach it; the number-word list is only accessible from the start
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as an error to correct — it matures with practice; play 'start here and keep going' from many points using a visible number track
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restarts at 1 rather than beginning at 23

errorPatterns.pattern: backward counting collapses — counts up fluently but counting back is halting, skips, or reverts to forward
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT expect backward to arrive with forward — it develops separately; practise short backward runs (5→0) with a number line and a physical step-down
errorPatterns.revealedBy: errors or reversion when counting back from 20

errorPatterns.pattern: omits or repeats a number in an otherwise ordered recite (…14, 15, 17…) — the number-name string itself is insecure
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill at speed — slow the pace and anchor on a hundred square, pointing to each; if the word string is broken, rebuild it gently rather than penalising
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an isolated missing or doubled word within the sequence

responseLevels.gap: Cannot recite an ordered sequence to 100 — omits/repeats numbers, breaks down at decade boundaries, or can only count forward from 1.
responseLevels.full: Counts 1–100 with no skips or repeats across decade boundaries, resumes forward from any given number, and counts back from 20 to 0 fluently.
responseLevels.partial: Recites 1–100 forward reliably but restarts from 1 when asked to begin at 23, or backward counting is halting — the sequence works as a forward chant only.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count out loud from 1, as far as you can, up to 100. Then I'll stop you and give a new place to start: begin at 23 and keep going. Last, count backwards from 20 down to 0. (Watch the decade boundaries, whether they can start mid-sequence, and whether backward counting holds.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Forward-from-1 alone hides the real breaks. Fluent rote counting shows at the decade boundaries, the start-at-23, and the count-back. A child whose counting is a single memorised chant restarts from 1 when asked to begin at 23, stalls or invents numbers at ten-crossings ('…29, twenty-ten' or '…39, 50'), or can only go forward — backward counting collapses.
